content.summary_of_the_paper:
Summary:

The paper proposes a new domain generalization paradigm called evolving domain generalization, where the source domains and the target domain are not random but have an evolving pattern.

The paper provides theoretical results on the evolving domain generalization, which bounds the target domain test error with synthetic domains.

The paper proposes a new approach for evolving domain generalization, which learns two embedding functions to derive the synthetic domains and minimize the distances between the synthetic domains and the real domains within the hidden space

The paper conducts experiments on three domain generalization datasets including RMNIST, Portrait, and Cover Type.
content.main_review:
Strength:

The paper proposes a new problem setting of evolving domain generalization and provides rigorous theoretical guarantees. 

The paper provides a new approach for evolving domain generalization based on the theoretical results.

The paper algorithm is easy to understand and clearly clarified.

The paper is organized in a fluent way.

Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on several domain generalization datasets.

Weakness:

My only worry for the paper is the practical value of the problem setting. All the experiments are done in a quite controlled setting, like the increasing rotation angles and different decades. However, in practical, I'm not sure when such controlled setting is useful.

Minor:

The citation here is broken: Finally, we note two key theoretical differences between DDG and DA in evolving environments [shai-ben, mingsheng long].

content.title: Thanks for your review!
content.comment:
We appreciate that you note the significance and novelty of our paper. The following is our response to your concern about the practical value of the problem setting.

1. **Evolving pattern across domains exists in real life commonly.** Examples include: a) Data collected over a long time period can be divided into different domains. With our approach, we can generate a model for future prediction. b) Geographically relevant datasets can be divided into different domains at different latitudes and longitudes, soil depths, and distances from water sources ... c) Medically relevant datasets can be divided according to the age of the patients. Usually, the data from patients at higher and lower ages are more difficult to collect, resulting in an uneven sample at both ends of the age spectrum. Our approach can provide a model for the age group with no samples. d) Any dataset that can be divided into multiple domains based on a particular feature can be applied. Then we can generate a model for the domains with no samples.
2. As a result, **such a problem has been actively studied in the literature**, and the related works have been published in top-tier venues recently [1-7] (Here, we only list several representative papers since 2019). These studies have demonstrated that leveraging evolving patterns between domains is beneficial and worth more exploration.
3. Existing studies mainly focus on the evolving domain adaptation problem, where the model still requires some instances from the target domain. In contrast, **we studied a more realistic (but more challenging) problem**, where the model has no to the target instances. Our problem setup is less restrictive, which significantly increases applicability of our method.
4. From the theoretical aspect, **our assumption on the environment is also milder and more realistic** than existing works. More discussions can be found in Section A.4 in Appendix.
5. We conducted extensive experiments on the benchmark datasets in in previous Evolving DA studies (such as RMNIST [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], EvolveCircle [1] and Portrait [2,4]) in our experiments. To better study the performance of our algorithm, we have introduced another large-scale satellite image dataset (FMoW). The experimental results further demonstrate the importance and effectiveness of leveraging evolving patterns in real-world scenarios.

[1] Wang, Hao, Hao He, and Dina Katabi. "Continuously indexed domain adaptation." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020.

[2] Kumar, Ananya, Tengyu Ma, and Percy Liang. "Understanding self-training for gradual domain adaptation." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020.

[3] Liu, Hong, et al. "Learning to Adapt to Evolving Domains." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2020).

[4] Chen, Hong-You, and Wei-Lun Chao. "Gradual Domain Adaptation without Indexed Intermediate Domains." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021).

[5] Chen, Yining, et al. "Active online learning with hidden shifting domains." International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. PMLR, 2021.

content.title: Thank your for your comments!
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments! Bellow is our response, and we hope it can further address your concern on the practical use of our method.

> For example, the transformation from age 10-20 to age 20-30 may not be the same as from age 20-30 to age 30-40.
> 

In fact, such scenario has already accommodated in our formulation. To see this, note that the transforming relationship can be approximated as $\mathcal D_{i+1}\approx g(\mathcal D_i)$. As $g$ is a deep neural networks, it can capture nonlinear (complex) relationship between domains. The quality of such approximation can be characterized by the notion of $\lambda$-consistency. 

In addition, as $g$ takes **$\mathcal{D}_{i}$** as input to "predict"  **$\mathcal{D}_{i+1}$,** it essentially already takes domain information into account, so that the transformation can be different for each domain. To see this, consider the EvolCircle dataset shown in Fig. 2. Since the evolutionary trajectory of instances forms a semicircle, the evolving direction from **$\mathcal D_i$** to **$\mathcal D_{i+1}$** is different for each evolving step.

> Although the method soundly solves the proposed problem, under such a made-up setting, the practical use of the method may not be high.
> 

As pointed out by Reviewers ZjwE and Hcay, learning in an evolving environment indeed exists in many real-world problems, and existing methods cannot handle it properly. We evaluated our algorithm on multiple real-world datasets, and the results show that DPNets consistently outperforms any other baselines by leveraging the evolving pattern. 

Moreover, we have also included a large scale satellite image classification dataset FMoW to demonstrate the performance of our algorithm under real-world setting. Specifically, we divide all samples into 19 domains according to the timeline that the images were taken. Then we use the first 18 domains as source to train a model for the unseen target. This is a valuable application scenario because we hope that the classification model can be deployed to the target images, but we can NEVER access them since the satellite images are collected over time.

The results are reported in the following table, and we can observe that DPNets largely outperforms other baselines by 5.6%-23.4%.

|  | DPNets(Ours) | ERM | Prototypical | DIRL | RSC | MTL | CORAL | Mixup | IRM | SD | VREx | SagNet | MMD | MLDG | GroupDRO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FMoW | 66.8 | 54.6 | 53.3 | 43.4 | 55.7 | 51.7 | 56.1 | 59.5 | 58.8 | 55.2 | 61.2 | 56.2 | 60.0 | 43.8 | 57.3 |

Machine learning under evolving environments has been extensively studied in previous works [1-9], which proves that evolving environment is widely considered to be a valuable problem setup. As for our Progressive Domain Generalization, the problem setup is much less restrictive than the previous Evolving Domain Adaptation [1-4] as we do not require access to the target domain.  Thus,ur problem setup has a broader range of applications.

---

[7] Ortiz-Jimenez, Guillermo, et al. "CDOT: Continuous Domain Adaptation using Optimal Transport." *arXiv preprint arXiv:1909.11448* (2019).

[8] Wulfmeier, Markus, Alex Bewley, and Ingmar Posner. "Incremental adversarial domain adaptation for continually changing environments." *2018 IEEE International conference on robotics and automation (ICRA)*. IEEE, 2018.

[9] Pentina, Anastasia, and Christoph H. Lampert. "Lifelong learning with non-iid tasks." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 28 (2015): 1540-1548.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In domain generalization (DG), we normally assume that the target domain is static rather than dynamic. However, we might meet many dynamic target domains in the real world (e.g., domains change over time), which will cause significant prediction errors on such dynamic target domains. To avoid this issue, this paper considers a new problem setting: directional DG (DDG), where target domains will dynamically change over time/rules/directions. 

To address this very challenging problem, this paper first analyses the property of DDG and defines the consistency between two near target domains. Based on this new definition, the authors propose a new generalization bound for the target domains. Such consistency definition also uses g* to connect all target domains and make the DDG solvable under some assumptions. Based on this bound, a meta-learning-inspired method is proposed to address DDG: directional prototypical network. Empirical evaluation on both synthetic and real-world data sets validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

In general, this paper contributes a novel problem setting and a valid solution to this setting. Although some motivations are unclear, the contributions of this paper are enough.
content.main_review:
Pros:

+ In the recent development of domain adaptation, researchers have noticed the situation where the target domain might change over time (e.g., images in daylight and night). Existing papers have also shown that this situation should be noticed because existing methods cannot handle it. In this paper, a new problem setting regarding DG is proposed along this line, which is novel and should be discussed in future.

+ The good contributions of this paper also lie in its theoretical analysis of this new problem setting. The theoretical parts of this paper are very clear and easy to follow. It demystifies the key assumptions behind the DDG. Based on the defined consistency, we can imagine when DDG is a valid problem, which is impressive.

+ This paper is easy to follow. Experiments can partially support the claims made in this paper. A plus should be that the performance gain of this proposed method is significant.

Cons:

- Although the theoretical part is very interesting and meaningful, the solution is not well-motivated. After reading the whole algorithm, I can follow the main idea of why you have such a design. However, I cannot follow the solution when I first read it. If we just delete the meta-learning concept, would it be better for understanding? It is better to connect your algorithm to your solution. 

- In Figure 3, could you draw the total performance of your method? It might be very close to 3(b), is that right?

- In all theorems, it seems that we can also try other distances to measure the discrepancy between two joint distributions? Is that possible to extend your theorems to more general ones? Some discussions might be needed here.

- I actually cannot follow Figure 2 well. I understand your algorithm by reading the text and algorithm table instead of Figure 2. Figure 2 should be redrawn or deleted. I think I cannot directly understand the support and query in this figure. They are from meta-learning rather than your key arguments.  
 
- One key reference is missing: gradually domain adaptation (ICML 2020). The whole idea of your paper is similar to this reference. Some discussions should be added to distinguish between your original contribution and the contributions of the reference.

- The difference between your paper and the Wang et al. (2020, CIDA) should be discussed deeply. The synthetic dataset used in your paper is the same one in Want et al. (2020), is that right?
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, considering the significance of the researched problem, this paper can be accepted by the ICLR2022. However, some points should be clarified and strengthened in the revision.

content.title: Thanks for your review!
content.comment:
Thanks for your thoughtful review! We appreciate that you are positive about our theoretical analysis and the experimental results. Please find below the answers to your comments and questions.

---

> Although the theoretical part is very interesting and meaningful, ... It is better to connect your algorithm to your solution.
> 

As suggested in strategy (iii) (see section 3.2). the rationale behind the meta-learning concept of our method is that we use the instances from the current domain $\mathcal{D}_i$ (i.e., the support set) to estimate the prototypes of the next domain  (i.e, the query set), which is consistent with the idea of the prototypical networks. In other words, we choose the prototypical networks because of the meta-learning nature of the problem. On the other hand, we would like to emphasize that our strategies in Section 3.2 for designing algorithms for evolving DG are quite general, and our solution is just one realization of the strategies. Other methods are also possible for this problem.

---

> In Figure 3, could you draw the total performance of your method? It might be very close to 3(b), is that right?
> 

We have added the overall the overall decision boundary to the figure, which is close to the ground truth, as expected.

---

> In all theorems, it seems that we can also try other distances to measure the discrepancy between two joint distributions? Is that possible to extend your theorems to more general ones? Some discussions might be needed here.
> 

While other distance metrics (e.g., total variation) could also work, we would emphasize that **the key point our theoretical analysis is the notion of $\lambda$-consistency and role of mapping function revealed by our analysis, rather than the metrics themselves.** On the other hand, it is not clear if H-divergence or Wasserstein distance would also work, since we do not know if Lemma 1 still hold for these metrics. Please also refer to our response to Reviewer TUL5 for more detailed discussion of our theoretical contributions.

---

> I actually cannot follow Figure 2 well. I understand your algorithm by reading the text and algorithm table instead of Figure 2. Figure 2 should be redrawn or deleted. I think I cannot directly understand the support and query in this figure. They are from meta-learning rather than your key arguments.
> 

Thanks for your comments, we have deleted Figure 2 (The overall architecture of DPNets) since it caused confusions. In addition, we add a new paragraph in Section 3.2 to discuss our algorithm. Please also refer to our response to Reviewer TUL5 for more detailed discussion of the connection between the connection between theory and our algorithm.

---

> One key reference is missing: gradually domain adaptation (ICML 2020). Some discussions should be added to distinguish between your original contribution and the contributions of the reference.
> 

Thank you for your suggestion. We agree that there should be more discussion about the paper you mentioned and other previous works. We have added further comparison to the assumptions of existing studies and ours at the Section A.4 of the appendix.

---

> The difference between your paper and the Wang et al. (2020, CIDA) should be discussed deeply. The synthetic dataset used in your paper is the same one in Want et al. (2020), is that right?
> 

The Portrait dataset was originally proposed in [1], and has been used as a benchmark dataset for studying evolving domain adaptation [2, 3] and other problems related to evolving domain [4, 5, 6, 7]. The synthetic dataset EvolCricle is from [8], which also study problem setup related to the evolving domains.

More discussion about the differences has been added to Section A.4 of the appendix.

---

display_title: Official Review of Paper2234 by Reviewer TUL5

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a domain generalization method that leverages the evolving pattern of the source domains. Specifically, if the source domains are collected as an ordered sequence with an evolving pattern (function), and if the target domain is the next in that sequence, then such a function can be learned (implicitly) to aid the learning of a new domain.
content.main_review:
- Strength: The idea of directional domain adaptation/domain generalization seems promising and definitely worth exploring more. The authors also demonstrate strong empirical results to support their method.
- Weaknesses:
    - The presentation of the paper is not clear. It introduces a (class of) function $g$ that transforms the data distribution among consecutive domains. However, it is not clear how: does it transform each data point from a domain to a data point of the other domain? Moreover, after the theoretical discussion, the function $g$ is not used in the practical implementation of the method, which makes the paper feel disconnected. 
    - The technical contribution of this paper is also limited. Based on the theorem by Shui et al., the paper presents a result regarding the loss term of the target domain, which is a direct collocation of an additional assumption about the consistency of the evolution of the domains. The assumption is also quite problematic, which I will get to later. Note also that there are similar results (to Shui et al.) in the DA and distribution shift literature with different divergence/distance metrics (total variation, H divergence, KL divergence), and I can see that the authors do not use the JS divergence in the implementation so I guess any other similar bound would work -- this is not a major concern but should be mentioned/discussed for completeness.
    - One of the major concerns is about the problem statement. Here we assume that there is a function that transforms between the domains, and the target domain is the next in that transformation. In that sense, the target domain is already determined/known. This goes against the problem setup of Domain Generalization, where the target domain is unknown/undetermined (people also usually talk about the loss term as average over a family of target domains/ worst case domain). This assumption is also too restricted, with application mostly to some toy/synthetic datasets (including RMNIST), and does not hold true for real-world datasets such as PACS and VLCS. I can see that this assumption can somewhat be accepted for data collected over a time period. However, even in that case, it is hard to believe that there is a single deterministic transformation function, as it might be probabilistic with some complex transformation mechanism: given the data of this year, there are countless possibilities how the next year's data will look like. We can also see from the bound that, when we can't learn/ when there doesn't exist a function g that transform the data distribution between the domain well (which is very likely given that the transformation is often probabilistic and complex), the RHS would be very large, making the bound vacuous. 
    - Regarding the implementation, the authors use two functions $f$'s instead of the transformation function $g$. It is confusing to me since these functions do not transform the data density between domains. The connection of this implementation to the earlier theoretical result should be clarified.
    - Regarding the experiments, although the results are strong, I feel like it is not a very fair comparison. The proposed method is privileged in the sense that it knows the order of the source domains (other methods are not given this information). However, this can be somewhat acceptable since this can be seen as a new direction and there are not many related baselines. I also suggest the authors to compare with [1,2], since they also use the concept of transformations among the domains, and discuss the similarities/differences. I am also not fully convinced about the result of ERM in Figure 3c, shouldn't the ERM fit the training data very well?

[1] Nguyen, A. Tuan, et al. "Domain Invariant Representation Learning with Domain Density Transformations." arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.05082 (2021).
[2] Robey, Alexander, George J. Pappas, and Hamed Hassani. "Model-Based Domain Generalization." arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.11436 (2021).
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the experiment results look promising, I am not fully convinced of the problem setup and the practicality of the assumptions made.

content.title: Thanks for your review! (1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for writing this meticulous review of our work! We're glad that you agree that “directional domain adaptation/domain generalization seems promising and definitely worth exploring more”. Here are responses for your questions.

---

> The presentation of the paper is not clear. ..., which makes the paper feel disconnected.
> 

DPNets **estimate the prototypes of the next domain $\mathcal{D}_{i+1}$** by leveraging the evolving information and instances from previous domain $\mathcal{D}_{i}$. In practice, DPNets perform such mapping in a representation space, and **$g$ consists of two mapping functions: $f_\phi$ and $f_\psi$.** We have re-organized our description of DPNets. Please refer to Section 3.2 for more details.

---

> The technical contribution of this paper is also limited. ... this is not a major concern but should be mentioned/discussed for completeness.
> 

Our theoretical result is not a direct collocation of Shui et al.

1. **Our major theoretical contribution is the introduction of the notion of** $\lambda$**-consistency,** which is novel and enables us to characterize the evolving pattern of a non-stationary environment by revealing the role of the mapping function. Please refer to our response to your next comment for more details.
2. **We study a totally different problem.** The theoretical results from Shui et al. (as well as all existing DA theoretical research) are based on the traditional DA setting, and cannot be directly applied in our problem setup. More specially, in the Shui et al, the bound is based on the distance between the source and the target domain, which cannot be applied to our problem, since the target data is not accessible. In contrast, our bound is based on the distances between real and synthetic domains of two consecutive source domains (the second term of Theorem 1), which reveals the importance of mapping function.
3. While other distance metrics (e.g., total variation) could also work, we would emphasize that the **key point our theoretical analysis is the notion of $\lambda$-consistency and role of mapping function revealed by our analysis**. On the other hand, it is not clear if H-divergence or Wasserstein distance would also work, since we do not know if Lemma 1 still hold for these metrics.

---

> One of the major concerns is about the problem statement. ... target domains/ worst case domain).
> 

We formulate the problem as a domain generalization problem since the algorithm does not have the access to any instances from the target domain. While we assume there exists an underlying transformation function $g^*$, **it is unknown and needs to be learned from the source data (there exists a function does NOT mean we know it)**. In fact, we believe that such a deterministic assumption is very common in the literature (e.g., assuming that there exists an underly labeling function, when analyzing the generalization performance of a hypothesis [1,2,3]). Thus, **the target domain is unknown (since** $g^*$ **is unknown even though we assume it exists).** Regarding the worst case, it is in fact the most significant benefit of our approach – by learning and leveraging the evolving pattern, we don’t need to consider the worst case, but the “most probable” case in the target domain.

Considering the suggestion from reviewer ZjwE, "the emphasis should be more consistent progression across multiple domain", we believe "Sequential Domain Generalization" would be a better name. But, anyway, the naming method does not affect the essence of the problem. 

> This assumption is also too restricted,  ... data collected over a time period.
> 

Our method cannot handle the datasets such as PACS and VLCS since we are studying a totally different problem in this paper. We believe such a problem has practical value and a similar problem has been actively studied in several very recent works [4, 5, 6, 7]. On the other hand, these works studied the domain adaptation problems in evolving environment, where the algorithms still had access to target data. In contrast, we address an even more realistic (less restrictive) but more challenging problem, since we do not use the target data at all. Also, we have introduced FMoW, a large scale satellite image dataset to demonstrate the practical value of our problem setup and algorithm.

content.title: Thanks for your review! (2/2)
content.comment:
> However, even in that case, it is hard to believe that there is a single deterministic transformation function, ... the RHS would be very large, making the bound vacuous.
> 

**Our theoretical results are exactly consistent with your example.** As we already mentioned in our paper, “capturing the evolving pattern in $\mathcal{E}$ is hopeless if it varies arbitrarily” (in the first sentence of the paragraph immediately before Definition 1 in Section 3.2). Indeed, **the notion of $\lambda$-consistency embodies your concern** – if the evolving pattern is too complex or probabilistic, even the best transformation function $g^*$  may still has a large $\lambda$. Then the RHS of Theorem 1 can be large, and we cannot expect to generalize well on a target domain (e.g., we do not expect that our algorithm can predict the stock market tomorrow). On the other hand, if the transformation function performs well, learning the in such a changing environment is possible by learning $g^*$ from source domains to minimize distance between **$\mathcal{D}_{i+1}^{g^\star}$**  and $\mathcal{D}_{i+1}$, as suggested in Theorem 1.  As an analogy, please refer to the notion of “combined error $\lambda$” and Theorem 2 in [2].

> Regarding the implementation, the authors use two functions 's ... should be clarified.
> 

DPNets use the instances from one domain to predict the prototypes of the next domain. In this sense, DPNets essentially minimizes the distance between **$\mathcal{D}^{g}_{i+1}(x|y)$** and $\mathcal{D}_{i+1}(x|y)$. Please refer to Section 3.2 for more details.

---

> Regarding the experiments, although the results are strong, I feel like it is not a very fair comparison. The proposed method is privileged ... a new direction and there are not many related baselines
> 

We agree that this deserves further investigation. To make a fair comparison, we tried three different strategies of adding domain information to the dataset. **(1) One dimension expanding; (2) One hot expanding; (3) Outer product.** To the best of our knowledge, this is the most common effective way of adding index information in machine learning. The experimental results fully demonstrate the advantage of our algorithm in exploiting evolving information. Details of the implementation and results of the different strategies can be found in **Section B.2 of the appendix**.

| Strategy | EvolCircle | RPlate | Average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ERM+No Domain Index | 72.7 | 63.9 | 68.3 |
| ERM+One-Dimension | 73.6 | 64.9 | 69.3 |
| ERM+One-Hot | 74.6 | 65.3 | 70.0 |
| ERM+Outer Product | 74.6 | 65.3 | 70.0 |
| DPNets (Ours) | 94.2 | 95.0 | 92.2 |

> I also suggest the authors to compare with [1, 2], since they also use the concept of transformations among the domains, and discuss the similarities/differences.
> 

Our target is to **estimate the prototypes of the next domain $\mathcal D_{i+1}$**  by leveraging the evolving information and samples from previous domain $\mathcal D_i$, which is fundamentally different from generating-based methods.

The ideas mentioned in your citations [8, 9] are inspirational, especially the second one, in which a new approach is proposed for joint probability alignment. They are both worth being involved in the experiment section and related work section. We have involved DIRL[8] as one our baseline. [9] is missing due to the difficulty of embedding the generation algorithm part of [9] into our framework.

|  | Average | EvolCircle | RPlate | RMNIST | Portrait | Cover Type | FMoW |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DIRL | 64.0 | 53.3 | 56.3 | 76.3 | 93.2 | 61.2 | 43.4 |
| ERM | 74.7 | 72.7 | 63.9 | 79.4 | 95.8 | 71.8 | 54.6 |
| DPNets (Ours) | 85.4 | 94.2 | 95.0 | 87.5 | 96.4 | 72.5 | 66.8 |

---

> I am also not fully convinced about the result of ERM in Figure 3c, shouldn't the ERM fit the training data very well?
> 

We use linear classifier for each algorithm in EvolvingCircle dataset. There is no single underlying linear classifier that can perform well on all domains as the boundary is half-circle. ERM and most traditional DG algorithms try to minimize average/worst-case accuracy on all domains so that the final single classifier would achieve high average/worst-case accuracy. While our target domain is at the "edge" of all domains, the learned linear classifier which can achieve high average/worst-case accuracy may fail in the target domain. So that traditional DG methods can not handle the EvolvingCircle dataset well. On the contrary, our DPNets can still achieve high accuracy as our mechanism allow us to generate a model specifically for the unseen target.

Also, we have followed the suggestion from reviewer Hcay  to "draw the total performance of our method", which is the classification results of samples of each domain with prototypes generated from immediately previous domain.

content.title: Discussion
content.comment:
I would like the thank the authors for their response. In this comment, I would like to focus on some major points first (we can discuss other minor points later).

- The first point is about the function $g$ (and the function class $\mathcal{G}$). Until now, I am still unsure what $g$ is (even after the rebuttal). Section 3.1 introduces this notation without properly explaining what that is. Specifically, $\mathcal{D}^{g}_{i+1}=g(\mathcal{D}_i)$. What does $g(\mathcal{D}_i)$ mean here? Can the author write the definition of $g$ and $g(\mathcal{D}_i)$ in a mathematically rigorous way so that the readers (including me) can follow and understand more easily?

- How $g$ can be replaced by $f_\phi$ and $f_\psi$? Maybe it will be easier to explain this after the above definitions that I mentioned.

- In general, I still feel like the assumption (or more like the problem setting) in this paper is too restricted (I am aware there are disagreements among the reviewers regarding this). I would recommend the authors to investigate in the following direction (for this paper or even for a future research direction, depending on the decision of this paper). Suppose that we do have an evolving pattern, but it is captured by a family (distribution) $E$ of transformations. Specifically, for all $t$, there exists $g \in E$ (or $g \sim E$ in case of distribution) such that $\mathcal{D}_{t+1} \approx g(\mathcal{D}_t)$. Then, the transformation is not arbitrary, but the setting still allows for a more flexible and probabilistic transformation. Can we do something to exploit and leverage this evolving pattern for the domain generalization problem?

content.title: Discussion
content.comment:
Thanks for your follow-up questions! I apologize for the confusion and hopefully our response could address your concerns, and we will revise our paper to clarify the notations accordingly based on your comments.

> The first point is about the function $g$ (and the function class $\mathcal G$). Until now, I am still unsure what $g$ is (even after the rebuttal). Section 3.1 introduces this notation without properly explaining what that is. Specifically, $\mathcal D_{i+1}^g=g(\mathcal D_i)$. What does $g(\mathcal D_i)$ mean here? Can the author write the definition of $g$ and $g(\mathcal D_i)$ in a mathematically rigorous way so that the readers (including me) can follow and understand more easily?
> 

In our theoretical analysis (Section 3.1), **$\mathcal{D}_i(x,y)$** is the joint probability distribution of the instance $x$ and its label $y$ that characterizes the $i$-th domain. Let **$(x,y) \sim \mathcal{D}_i$,** and **$\mathcal D^g_{i+1}(x,y) \triangleq \mathcal{D}_i(g(x),y)$,** $g \in \mathcal{G}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$ is a (deterministic) mapping function. Accordingly, $\mathcal{G}$ is a family of mapping functions (In our paper, we wrote **$\mathcal D^g_{i+1} =g(\mathcal{D}_i)$** to express the same meaning, which is not entirely formally correct and cause the confusion. We will fix this issue in our revision). Ideally, we hope that **$\mathcal D^g_
{i+1}$** is close to **$\mathcal D_{i+1}$** as much as possible.

---

> How g can be replaced by  $f_ϕ$ and $f_ψ$? Maybe it will be easier to explain this after the above definitions that I mentioned.
> 

Our theoretical results indicate that one should minimize the distance between **$\mathcal{D}_{i+1}^g(x,y)$** and **$\mathcal{D}_{i+1} (x,y)$** (e.g., the synthetic and real distributions) over domains. In addition, if we further assume that there is no label shift (i.e., **$\mathcal{D}_i(y)$’s** are all the same), then, we only need to align **$\mathcal{D}_{i+1}^g(x|y) \triangleq \mathcal{D}_i(g(x)|y)$** and **$\mathcal{D}_{i+1} (x|y)$**, as discussed in Remark 3. In our practical implementation, such an alignment is achieved by prototypical networks in the feature space $\mathcal{Z}$. The rationale behind it is that the prototypes can be viewed as the centroid of instances of each class, which is an approximation of the semantic conditional distribution of each class [11, 12]. Therefore, instead of learning $g: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, we learn **$g: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$** in a way such that after mapping, the prototypes of the $i+1$-th task can be estimated from instances of the $i$-th task. More specifically, $g$ consists of two components:  $f_\phi, f_\psi: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$. Let $x^i$ be an instance from **$\mathcal{D}_i$** and $x^{i+1}$ be an instance from **$\mathcal{D}_{i+1}$,** we pass $x^i$ through $f_\phi$ ($f_\phi$ is the implementation of $g$) and $x^{i+1}$ through $f_\psi$ so that we can use $f_\phi(x^i)$ (i.e., the instances from $i$-th domain) to estimate the prototypes of $f_\psi(x^{i+1})$ (i.e., the prototypes of the $i+1$-domain) in the feature space $\mathcal{Z}$.

---

> In general, I still feel like the assumption (or more like the problem setting) in this paper is too restricted ... Suppose that we do have an evolving pattern, but it is captured by a family (distribution) $E$ of transformations. Specifically, for all $t$, there exists $g∈E$ (or $g∼E$ in case of distribution) such that $\mathcal D_{t+1}≈g(\mathcal D_t)$. Then, the transformation is not arbitrary, but the setting still allows for a more flexible and probabilistic transformation. Can we do something to exploit and leverage this evolving pattern for the domain generalization problem?
> 

We appreciate your suggestion on the probabilistic transformation of the evolving pattern. We do believe that this could be our direction for future work. In this work, we show that when learning in an evolving environment, the learning performance can indeed be improved by leveraging the evolving pattern (even though our assumption may be restrictive for real-world problems). We highlight the role of capturing the evolving pattern, and our method is just one approach to it. The probabilistic approach is definitely worth exploring. Regarding your question, we are not experts in probabilistic machine learning, but possible solutions may include Bayesian neural networks and deep Gaussian processes, which can capture and uncertainty of the transformation and/or the environment.

---

[11] Xie, Shaoan, et al. "Learning semantic representations for unsupervised domain adaptation." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2018.

[12] Shui, Changjian, et al. "Aggregating From Multiple Target-Shifted Sources." arXiv preprint arXiv:2105.04051 (2021).

display_title: Official Review of Paper2234 by Reviewer ZjwE

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the issue of training a model to generalize to data from unseen domains when there is a natural progression between domain at training and test time (eg. temporal progression). With the assumption that there is a fixed underlying transformation "g" which underlies the evolution of the data distributions, they propose a training algorithm based on progressive net which simultaneously learns g as well as well as a strong classifier. The resulting model can be used on unseen domains at test-time, leveraging the learned transformation to extrapolate to the new domain.
content.main_review:
The paper proposes a sensible solution to tackle an interesting and relatively under-studied problem. Strong experimental results support the adequacy of the proposed approach on a variety of benchmarks. However, some missing baselines/ablation make it hard to interpret these results as a consequence of the proposed training algorithm as opposed to the choice of the classifier (prototypical networks). Until this is particular point is resolved, my recommendation is that the paper is borderline.

Pros:
- The paper tackles an interesting and under-studied problem, which has many concrete applications in the real world
- The problem itself is overall well-framed, as are the assumptions and use-cases of the method are clearly delineated
- Experimental results are convincingly in favor of DPNets

Cons:
- Lack of comparison to prototypical nets. As far as I can tell, there is no direct comparison with a "non-directional" version of prototypical nets. This makes it difficult to disentangle the effect of the proposed "directional learning" algorithm from the superior expressive power of PNets granted by their transductive nature.
- I am not particularly fond of the task of gender prediction from teenage faces across decades (referred to as "Portrait" in the paper). What is  the intended use-case of this particular application? And what leads the authors to believe that this is an appropriate benchmark for DPNet specifically (ie what is the "g" function in that case)? I think this should at least be addressed in the paper or in the ethics statement (note that the authors didn't include the latter). If the purpose was to demonstrate the efficacy of the approach on a realistic, time-stratified image recognition benchmark, my personal opinion is that something like the FMoW dataset (https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.07846) would have been a better, and less questionable choice.

Additional comments:
- There is a rather substantial body of work on distributionally robust optimization which is largely ignored in the intro/related work section. The authors do compare against group-DRO (from Sagawa et al. 2020), but I think the broader DRO literature should be acknowledged elsewhere in the paper (eg. first paragraph of Sec.2)
- For some reason I am not 100% sold on the name "directional domain generalization". To me the emphasis should be less on the "direction" or "directedness" of the procedure but rather on the consistent progression across multiple domain. In my opinion, something like "progressive" or "sequential" domain generalization would be more adequate.
- There is a typo in citations towars the end of page 4 ("[shai-ben, mingsheng long]")
- I think figure 5 would be better as a 2d heatmap with "distance of domains" and "# of domains" as the two axes and the relative differences should be shown only as colors (and perhaps numerically). The elevation doesn't add much and the perspective makes reading the results along the 3 axes awkward.
- In Table 2, I would expect that the performance of DPNet monotonically increases as the number of domains gets larger (since we can learn a more accurate "g"). However, this is not the case, in particular for 13 domains, the performance of DPNet plummets and is even worse than for 3 domains. Could the authors explain this counter intuitive result? The standard deviation is rather small so it doesn't seem like this is just an issue of variance due to the random seed
- Similarly in Table 2 I am not sure if I understand why the performance of ERM drops when there are more domains. Shouldn't the addition of multiple domains act as "data augmentation" for ERM? If I understand correctly, for 19 domains, ERM minimizes the loss on 19 different rotations of MNIST, which should encourage it to learn rotation invariant representations. Can the authors clarify the experimental setting and explain this failure of ERM?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a sensible solution to tackle an interesting and relatively under-studied problem. Strong experimental results support the adequacy of the proposed approach on a variety of benchmarks. However, some missing baselines/ablation make it hard to interpret these results as a consequence of the proposed training algorithm as opposed to the choice of the classifier (prototypical networks). Until this is particular point is resolved, my recommendation is that the paper is borderline.

content.title: Thanks for your review! (1/2)
content.comment:
Thanks for your thoughtful review! We're glad that you find our approach "a sensible solution to tackle an interesting and relatively under-studied problem". We have revised our paper based on your suggestions to more it more concrete. The following are responses to your concerns.

---

> Lack of comparison to prototypical nets. ... by their transductive nature.
> 

Thanks for your suggestion. We have included the original "non-directional" prototypical nets (i.e., we randomly select the support and query sets) as one of our baselines, and the results are added in Table 1. It can be observed that DPNets consistently outperforms the prototypical nets, which justifies the benefits of learning the evolving patterns. To further compare DPNets and the prototypical nets, we also add t-SNE illustrations of the prototypical nets in Fig. 6. The results further demonstrate that both ERM and the original prototypical network cannot capture the evolving pattern. While our approach is able to take advantage of the evolving information to improve the performance.

|  | EvolCircle | RPlate | RMNIST | Portrait | Cover Type | FMoW | Average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prototypical | 93.6 | 66.3 | 85.2 | 96.2 | 66.5 | 53.3 | 76.9 |
| ERM | 72.7 | 63.9 | 79.4 | 95.8 | 71.8 | 54.6 | 74.7 |
| DPNets (Ours) | 94.2 | 95.0 | 87.5 | 96.4 | 72.5 | 66.8 | 85.4 |

> I am not particularly fond of the task of gender prediction from teenage faces ... would have been a better, and less questionable choice.
> 

We apologize for the potential negative impact. We adopt the portrait dataset only for demonstrating the effectiveness of our method. This dataset was originally proposed in [1], and has been used as a benchmark dataset for studying evolving domain adaptation [2, 3] and other problems related to evolving domain [4, 5, 6, 7]. The function $g$ is to capture the style elements, or trends in fashion and social norms over time. We have added an ethics statement in our paper to address this issue.
In addition, we also included the FMoW dataset as an additional benchmark in our experiments. Due to the time and computational resource limits, we only select 5 common classes to compose a classification task, and the results are shown in Table 1. We can observe that DPNets still outperforms other baselines on this dataset.

|  | DPNets(Ours) | ERM | Prototypical | DIRL | RSC | MTL | CORAL | Mixup | IRM | SD | VREx | SagNet | MMD | MLDG | GroupDRO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FMoW | 66.8 | 54.6 | 53.3 | 43.4 | 55.7 | 51.7 | 56.1 | 59.5 | 58.8 | 55.2 | 61.2 | 56.2 | 60.0 | 43.8 | 57.3 |

content.title: Thanks for your review! (2/2)
content.comment:
> broader DRO literature should be acknowledged elsewhere in the paper
> 

We have added DRO and some other methods including gradient operation, self-supervision, and random forest in Related Work - Domain Generalization (DG) - Line 19 to 21.

> For some reason I am not 100% sold on the name "directional domain generalization" ... would be more adequate.
> 

Thanks for your suggestion. We have renamed our problem as “Progressive Domain Generalization”

> There is a typo in citations towars the end of page 4 ("[shai-ben, mingsheng long]")
> 

Thank you for pointing it out, we have fixed the typo.

> I think figure 5 would be better as a 2d heatmap
> 

Thanks for your suggestion, we have re-plotted the figure.

> In Table 2, I would expect that the performance of DPNet monotonically increases ... variance due to the random seed.
> 

First, we apologize that there was a typo in Table 2, where the accuracy of DPNets should be 87.3 (not 81.3). We further we conduct additional experiments in Section B.1 of the Appendix, where we vary both the number of domains and the domain distance, and the results are shown in Figure 6 (green lines). We can observe from the averaged performance (over the domain distances) that **the overall trend of the green line is still going up as the number of domains increases.** On the other hand, we also conjecture that the evolving pattern of RMNIST is relatively simple. Thus, a small number of domains are sufficient to learn such a pattern, and increasing the number of domains may not necessarily improve the performances of DPNets anymore. This can be observed from Figs 6a&6b vs Fig 6c – the trend is even less obvious when the distance is smaller (i.e., degree 3 and degree 7).

> Similarly in Table 2 I am not sure if I understand why the performance of ERM drops ... explain this failure of ERM?
> 

This is a great question, which is exactly consistent with the motivation of our work. We believe this is because the target domain in our experimental setup is $\mathcal{D}_{i+1}$ (i.e., we perform “extrapolation”), and having more domains does not necessarily help learn an invariant representation if we do not leverage the evolving pattern. Intuitively, as the target domain is on the “edge” of the domains, having more domains also indicates that it is further away from the “center” of the source domains, which may even make the generalization even more challenging. On the other hand, if the target domain is “among” the source domains (i.e., we perform ”interpolation”), the source domains may act as augmented data which improve the generalization performance. To verify our idea, we compare the generalization performances of both extrapolation (orange lines) and interpolation (green lines, where we choose the domain in the middle as the target domain), and the results are shown in Figure 6. We can observe that the results align with our intuition – more source domains will be beneficial for ”interpolation” but not necessarily for “extrapolation”.

---

[1] A Century of Portraits: A Visual Historical Record of American High School Yearbooks

[2] Kumar, Ananya, Tengyu Ma, and Percy Liang. "Understanding self-training for gradual domain adaptation." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020.

[3] Chen, Hong-You, and Wei-Lun Chao. "Gradual Domain Adaptation without Indexed Intermediate Domains." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021).

[4] Chen, Yining, et al. "Active online learning with hidden shifting domains." International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. PMLR, 2021.

[5] Zhou, Shiji, et al. "Online Continual Adaptation with Active Self-Training." arXiv preprint arXiv:2106.06526 (2021).

[6] Mancini, Massimiliano, et al. "Adagraph: Unifying predictive and continuous domain adaptation through graphs." *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition*. 2019.

[7] Lei, Qi, Wei Hu, and Jason Lee. "Near-optimal linear regression under distribution shift." *International Conference on Machine Learning*. PMLR, 2021.

content.title: My concerns are addressed & follow up comments
content.comment:
I would like to thank the authors for their detailed response which have clarified most of my concerns regarding the paper. I think it is now in a good place, and would be a valuable contribution to the field.

In particular I disagree with Reviewer TUL5 (and VdAQ) that the paper's assumptions are too unrealistic (or that the setting is "too made up") to be of interest to the community.

I think the authors do a good job of motivating why this assumption might be reasonable in practice in some cases, and the paper provides convincing empirical evidence that a method based on this assumption is able to outperform many baselines even in settings that are not synthetic. I fully agree with Reviewer's Hcay comments.

I raised my score to 8 and I vote to accept the paper.
